doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: American Jazz Orchestra, Central City Sketches and Helen Merrill at the Vanguard
summary: Six years with the American Jazz Orchestra under John Lewis, the Ellington triptych, the 1987 Carter concert, and Thad Jones at the Vanguard.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: So what did you decide to play in that spot in the Thad Jones?

I’ll never — I can’t remember. Another time I also had a very pleasing experience for about six years from 1986 to about ’91, ’92 with the American Jazz Orchestra, which is a wonderful repertory orchestra that was started by Gary Giddins and we played at Cooper Union and John Lewis was the musical director, and Gunther came in one time and we did an Ellington triptych, well that was a trying experience with him because Gunther, if you see this I’m going to complain because I had a terrible time reading Duke’s comp, where he wrote out the comp.

It came out, anyhow, I thought it came out good. I listened to those tapes recently, they sound pretty good. But it was very trying to read that kind of stuff. And some guys just read that right off. I’m not a world class reader. I can read, particularly if I get a little peek at it ahead of time I’m okay, but I’m not a studio style sight reader. There were some trying moments with John, we had a misunderstanding about whether I was supposed to play or not at a Dizzy concert and I wound up playing and he told me, never mind. I mumbled through this one. We smoothed it out. The most exciting time with the orchestra was in 1987 they invited Benny Carter to come and conduct a concert entirely of his music and write a new suite for the occasion. And the album, and we did it, a wonderful concert, everybody played great and then we went in the studio and did the album which is still available, which I highly recommend, it’s called “Central City Sketches.” American Jazz Orchestra. I’m pretty pleased with my part in that. And I’d like to mention something that was a highlight of my recording career, I’d like to mention. In the 60s I got involved with a wonderful singer named Helen Merrill. And we used to work a lot in those days, you know we used to work at the Vanguard. One time I had a gig there, this is an interesting story, it was Helen and I and my trio with Ben Riley, who’s, he’s my favorite right now, and a wonderful bass player named Tommy Williams who has since passed away. The other attraction was the Bill Evans Trio. Okay? And we had a quartet which included Thad Jones. We had been there a week and Max Gordon says, “The trumpet player plays funny,” he says, “we don’t’ really need him, do we?” He says, “What do you need a trumpet for?” You know Bill Evans is there. Why don’t you — I said sorry, it’s not about to happen, I’m not going fire Thad Jones. He said, “Well I think Ben Webster is available.” No. Sorry. I can’t do that. So we got together and we said to Thad we’ll pay your salary, we’ll both chip in, if you stay. And Thad says no. And he didn’t play the second week.
